sections.title: The Mitzva
sections.html:
Israel is commanded to separate terumot and ma'asrot (priestly gifts and tithes) from the grain and fruit that they grow in the Land of Israel. The mitzva comprises four components: two of teruma and two of ma'aser. That is why it is called "terumot u-ma'asrot" – two terumot and two ma'asrot. The terumot are holy and are designated for the kohanim, who must eat them in a state of purity. "Ma'aser rishon" (the first tithe) is designated for the Levites, and since it has no sanctity, it may be eaten without restriction. The purpose of the additional tithe changes according to the years of the Shemita cycle. In years 1, 2, 4 and 5 it is called "ma'aser sheni" (the second tithe), and it is brought up to Jerusalem and eaten there in purity. In years 3 and 6 it is given to the poor, and then it is called "ma'aser ani" (the poor man's tithe), and since it has no sanctity, it may be eaten without restriction.

Since the Temple was destroyed, we are unable to fulfill the mitzva of terumot u-ma'asrot properly. First, the kohanim cannot eat terumot, because the terumot must be eaten in purity, and today all people, including the kohanim, are considered impure with corpse impurity. For any person who touched a corpse, or was under one roof with a corpse, or touched a metal vessel that touched a corpse, is impure, and only through the procedure of sprinkling the water of the ashes of the red heifer can he become pure; and as a result of the destruction of the Temple and the exile, the purification procedure has been lost to us. Second, the fruit of ma'aser sheni must be eaten in purity in Jerusalem near the altar, and in addition to the fact that we cannot become pure, the Temple and the altar have been destroyed. There is also a problem with regard to ma'aser rishon, which is designated for the Levites, for since the destruction, the service of the kohanim and Levites in the Temple has ceased, and since there is no need to check their lineage, consequently, when one wishes to give them the tithe, there is a certain doubt regarding their lineage. In practice, however, one must fulfill it and give it to Levites who are engaged in Torah study (below 9:8). The only tithe that can be fulfilled today, ab initio, without any doubt, is ma'aser ani, which must be separated in years 3 and 6 of the Shemita cycle. (In addition, since most of the Jewish people are in the Diaspora, according to most poskim the mitzva today is only rabbinic, as explained below 12:11.)

In practice, even though the original purpose of terumot u-ma'asrot finds almost no expression today, the obligation of the mitzva has not been annulled, and by fulfilling it we remember the great vision hidden within it, and the foods we eat are sanctified by being connected to holy values. As long as terumot u-ma'asrot have not been separated from the produce, it is forbidden to eat it, and in the language of the Sages it is called "tevel," which means "tov-lo" ("not good"), that is, it is not fit to be eaten; it is likewise forbidden to use it for sowing (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 6:3).

In this chapter we will explain the principles of the mitzva and its reasons as it ought to be fulfilled ab initio in an ideal state, and in the following chapters we will explain the principles of the halakhot and the ways they are fulfilled nowadays.

sections.title: The Order of Fulfilling the Mitzva in Its Four Parts
sections.html:
It is a Torah mitzva to separate terumot u-ma'asrot in their proper order (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 3:23). First, one must separate "teruma gedola" (the great teruma) for the kohen, as it was said to Aharon the kohen (Bamidbar 18:12): "All the best of the oil, and all the best of the wine and of the grain, the first part of them which they give to the Lord, to you have I given them." By Torah law, teruma gedola has no fixed amount, and each person may give as much as he pleases; even if he gives one grain of wheat from the entire threshing floor, he has fulfilled the mitzva. But the Sages set an amount for it, and enacted that an ordinary person should separate one-fiftieth of the produce (2%); those with a "stingy eye," who are sparing with their money, should separate one-sixtieth (1.67%); and those with a "generous eye" should separate one-fortieth (2.5%). It is a mitzva to separate teruma gedola by estimate, so that the desire of the heart will find expression in it; therefore, even after the Sages instituted an amount for teruma gedola, they ruled that it should be separated by estimate, without weighing, measuring or counting the produce (Yerushalmi Terumot 1:4, based on Bamidbar 18:27).

2) Ma'aser rishon: afterwards one separates a tenth of the remaining produce for the Levite, as it is stated (Bamidbar 18:21): "And to the children of Levi, behold, I have given all the tithe in Israel for an inheritance, in return for their service which they serve, the service of the Tent of Meeting."

3) Terumat ma'aser: from the tithe given to the Levite, the Levite must separate a tithe, which is a tithe of the tithe, and give it to the kohen. As it is stated (ibid. 26-28): "And you shall speak to the Levites and say to them: When you take from the children of Israel the tithe which I have given you from them as your inheritance, then you shall set apart from it a gift for the Lord, a tithe of the tithe… the Lord's gift to Aharon the kohen." After the separation of terumat ma'aser, about nine percent of all the produce would remain in the Levite's hands, while the kohen would receive about three percent of the produce from the two terumot.

4) After the separation of ma'aser rishon, another tithe is separated from the remaining produce. In years 1, 2, 4 and 5 of the Shemita cycle it is called ma'aser sheni, and it remains in the hands of the owner of the produce, who must bring it up to Jerusalem and eat it there in purity. In years 3 and 6 this tithe is called ma'aser ani and is given to the poor.

The ideal structure of the Israelite nation, as a nation whose feet are planted in the earth and whose head reaches the heights of heaven, rests to a great extent on the mitzva of terumot u-ma'asrot, which creates a strong bond between the world of action and the world of the spirit, between those engaged in work and those engaged in Torah and education. Thanks to the terumot and ma'aser rishon that the people of action separated from their harvest, the kohanim and Levites were able to devote themselves to spiritual service, and thus the people of action and the people of the spirit became partners in sustaining a life full of meaning.

Not only that, but terumot u-ma'asrot reveal the holy values hidden in the produce that grows in the Land of Israel. Through giving terumot to the kohanim, the yearning to assist the holy service and to magnify Torah in Israel finds expression. Through ma'aser rishon to the Levite, the aspiration to assist the work of education and the teaching of Torah is revealed. In the four years in which we separate ma'aser sheni, the aspiration of every Jew to be personally connected to holiness, through going up to Jerusalem and eating his produce in purity, is revealed. And there is another aspiration hidden in the produce – to help the poor – and it finds expression in the two years in which ma'aser ani is separated (as well as in leaving leket, shikheḥa and pe'a – gleanings, forgotten sheaves and the corner of the field – for the poor). After all these values have found expression, the produce becomes fit and suitable for eating, adding strength and joy to Israel for a good life.

sections.title: Upholding the Torah in Israel
sections.html:
The role of the kohanim and Levites is to be the people of Torah and education in Israel, as it is stated (Devarim 33:10): "They shall teach Yaakov Your ordinances, and Israel Your Torah." And it is also stated (ibid. 17:8-9): "If a matter of judgment is too hard for you, between blood and blood, between plea and plea, and between affliction and affliction, matters of controversy within your gates, then you shall arise and go up to the place which the Lord your God shall choose. And you shall come to the kohanim, the Levites, and to the judge who shall be in those days, and you shall inquire, and they shall tell you the word of judgment." So that the kohanim and Levites would be spread throughout the land and free for their spiritual work, to study Torah and to teach it, the Torah established that they would not be given an inheritance in the land; rather, each and every tribe would allot them cities within its inheritance. As it is stated (Bamidbar 35:1-8): "And the Lord spoke to Moshe… Command the children of Israel that they give to the Levites, from the inheritance of their possession, cities to dwell in, and open land around the cities you shall give to the Levites. And the cities shall be theirs to dwell in, and their open land shall be for their cattle, for their possessions, and for all their animals… All the cities that you shall give to the Levites shall be forty-eight cities… from the many you shall take many, and from the few you shall take few; each according to the inheritance which he inherits shall give of his cities to the Levites." That is, the kohanim and Levites received places to live, and even open land for their possessions, but they did not receive land on which to grow their food; rather, they were sustained by the terumot and ma'asrot that they received from Israel. As it is stated (Devarim 18:1-2): "The kohanim, the Levites, all the tribe of Levi, shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel; they shall eat the fire-offerings of the Lord and His inheritance. And they shall have no inheritance among their brethren; the Lord is their inheritance, as He has spoken to them." And so did Israel do in the days of Yehoshua, as it is stated (Yehoshua 21:3): "And the children of Israel gave to the Levites from their inheritance, at the command of the Lord, these cities and their open lands…" Over the generations, as needed, additional cities were allotted to the kohanim and Levites, such as Nov and Anatot.

Since the purpose of the terumot for the kohanim and the tithe for the Levites is to assist them in their spiritual role, it is a mitzva to give them to kohanim and Levites who are Torah scholars, who study and teach Torah. As King Ḥizkiyahu instructed (II Divrei Ha-yamim 31:4): "Moreover he commanded the people who dwelt in Jerusalem to give the portion of the kohanim and the Levites, so that they might hold fast to the Torah of the Lord."

If there were no kohanim and Levites there who were engaged in Torah, the obligation remained in place, and one must give the terumot and the tithe to kohanim and Levites who are not Torah scholars, because the whole tribe was designated for this, since it has no inheritance in the land. And even if the gifts are temporarily given to those who are not Torah scholars, as soon as kohanim and Levites who are Torah scholars arrive there, one should return to giving the gifts to them.1

Beyond the fact that the tribe of Levi was designated as responsible for the study and teaching of Torah in Israel, any Jew who desired it was permitted to devote his life to Torah, to learning and to teaching (Rambam, Hilkhot Shemita Ve-yovel 13:13). Since the terumot u-ma'asrot were not intended for them, the Israelites who wished to do so had to reduce their work in their fields and make do with little in order to be free for Torah study. Presumably those who chose this were outstanding in talent, diligence and good character, and consequently they merited to reach high levels of Torah knowledge, beyond the average of the members of the tribe of Levi, so that many of them served as heads of yeshivot and as members of the courts and of the Sanhedrin. Sometimes their family members helped them earn their livelihood, like Zevulun and Yissakhar, and sometimes the public paid them compensation for lost work time so that they would devote their time to teaching or to judging. Even so, the important role of the members of the tribe of Levi remained in place, for upon them was placed the overall responsibility for upholding the Torah in Israel: educating young and older children, setting regular times for classes with adults, making peace between a person and his fellow and between husband and wife, giving emotional support to those in need, and rehabilitating murderers and criminals. On top of this solid foundation, the Israelites who devoted themselves to Torah added an important layer to magnifying and glorifying the Torah, in halakhic ruling, education and the enrichment of social life in all the areas in which the members of the tribe of Levi were engaged. (The enactment of ma'aser kesafim – tithing money – continues the purpose of terumot u-ma'asrot from the realm of agriculture to other occupations and businesses.)

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: The Distribution of the Gifts
sections.html:
The owner of the produce retains the right to choose to which kohen he will give his terumot and to which Levite he will give his ma'asrot, as it is stated (Bamidbar 5:10): "And every man's hallowed things shall be his; whatever any man gives the kohen, it shall be his." This right created a personal bond between the Israelites and the kohanim and Levites, and spurred the kohanim and Levites to be devoted to the holy service among the members of their communities, so that the members of the community, for their part, would want to grant them their gifts. Whoever exerted himself to teach Torah to children and adults, and from whom people benefited in counsel and wisdom, merited that they would prefer to give him the gifts. Conversely, whoever was estranged from the members of his community, or acted haughtily towards them, or was lazy and did not teach Torah, received similar treatment at the time the gifts were distributed.

After the kohen has received the teruma produce, it is his property, and he may sell it to kohanim who will eat it in purity, and with the money he receives he may buy whatever he wishes (Ḥullin 131a). However, since it is forbidden for a kohen to trade in terumot (Mishna Shevi'it 7:3), a situation was not supposed to arise in which kohanim and Levites whom the public loved and honored for their wisdom and devotion would receive too many gifts, while their colleagues would receive none at all. For the gifts were foodstuffs, and after the admired kohanim and Levites had received all their needs in abundance, there was no point in giving them more gifts that their families could not eat. It was better for the owner of the produce to form a connection with other kohanim and Levites, who were more available to form a spiritual and educational bond with whoever chose to give them his gifts. Thus a continuous bond was created between all the Israelites and all the kohanim and Levites, with the devoted kohanim and Levites receiving preference and receiving all their needs first and in abundance, while those who were less welcoming, and did not exert themselves to teach their students well, received fewer gifts. And when hard years came and the harvest was meager, and the gifts were not enough to sustain all the kohanim and Levites, those who had not served the members of their communities properly suffered want.

The accepted practice was that the kohanim and Levites who were connected to the owner of the produce would come to the place where the produce was gathered in the fields to receive their gifts, because the obligation of the owner of the produce is to separate terumot u-ma'asrot, not to transport them to the homes of the kohen and the Levite. When the kohen and Levite did not come to the field, the Sages enacted that the owner of the produce should bring them to the homes of the kohen and Levite or hire a worker to do so, and the kohen and Levite would pay the price customarily paid for transport (Ḥullin 134b; Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 12:17). Presumably, when the owner of the field wished to give his gifts to a kohen or Levite who was great in Torah, he would volunteer to bring them to his home, so as not to take him away from Torah study.

It is forbidden for kohanim and Levites to take the gifts without permission, and it is likewise forbidden for them to help the owner of the produce with his work so that he will give them his gifts, because by doing so they deprive their brethren and desecrate the name of Heaven. Those who do so degrade their holy role, and they are presumed also not to teach Torah properly, and about them the prophet said (Malakhi 2:8-9): "But you have turned aside from the way; you have caused many to stumble in the Torah; you have corrupted the covenant of Levi, says the Lord of Hosts. Therefore I have also made you contemptible and base before all the people, according as you have not kept My ways, but have shown partiality in the Torah." It is also forbidden for kohanim and Levites to request the terumot or the tithe in an undignified manner, because these gifts are the Lord's, and He commanded that they be given to them in a dignified manner, as it is stated (Bamidbar 18:8): "And I, behold, I have given you the charge of My terumot, of all the hallowed things of the children of Israel; to you have I given them for distinction (le-moshḥa)." Le-moshḥa means greatness and honor, so that they will be able to teach Torah with dignity, as it is stated (Malakhi 2:7): "For the lips of the kohen shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek Torah from his mouth, for he is the messenger of the Lord of Hosts" (Bekhorot 26b; Tosafot 51b, s.v. "Ha-lakhakh"; Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 12:18-19).2

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Some Laws of Eating Terumot
sections.html:
The kohen, his wife and his children eat terumot. Thus it is not only the kohen alone who belongs to the holy service; rather, his whole family shares in his mission, and they too were required to keep the laws of purity in order to eat terumot.

The daughter of a kohen who married a zar (non-kohen), that is, an Israelite or a Levite, stops eating teruma. If she was widowed or divorced, and she had no son or daughter from him, she returns to her father's house and eats teruma; and if she had a child from him, she does not eat teruma. As it is stated (Vayikra 22:12-13): "And if a kohen's daughter is married to a zar, she shall not eat of the teruma of the holy things. But if a kohen's daughter is a widow or divorced, and has no child, and has returned to her father's house as in her youth, she shall eat of her father's bread." And likewise the reverse: an Israelite's daughter who married a kohen eats teruma with him. If she was widowed or divorced, if she has no descendant from him, she reverts to being an Israelite and does not eat teruma. And if she was left with a descendant from him, even a grandson or granddaughter, she remains of priestly status with him. And if she marries an Israelite, even though she has a child who is a kohen, she stops eating teruma (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 6:7-12; 17).

Before eating teruma, in addition to the blessing over enjoyment, the kohanim recite: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with the holiness of Aharon and commanded us to eat teruma" (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 15:22).

Teruma is given for eating, drinking and anointing the body: to eat something that is normally eaten, to drink something that is normally drunk, and to anoint with oil that is normally used to anoint the body. But one may not anoint his body with wine, since it is not customary to anoint the body with wine. Likewise, it is forbidden to eat or drink teruma in an unusual manner, for one who does so is considered to be wasting the teruma and transgresses a prohibition (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 11:1-9; see Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it 4:1, n. 1).3

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Purity and Impurity in Terumot
sections.html:
The role of the kohanim is to connect Israel to God, and keeping purity is one of the conditions for fulfilling their role; therefore only a pure kohen may eat teruma. For this purpose, the families of the kohanim and their children had to take care not to become impure, and also to protect their clothing and their vessels from becoming impure. The laws of purity and impurity are very numerous and complex, and we will mention a few of them:

In general, impurity is connected to death; therefore the corpse is the "avi avot ha-tum'a" (the ultimate source of impurity). A Jew or a vessel that touches a corpse or is with it in an "ohel," that is, under one roof, becomes an "av ha-tum'a" (primary source of impurity). For a Jew who became impure from a corpse to become pure, he must count seven days, and water of the ashes of the red heifer is sprinkled on him on the third and seventh days, and on the seventh day he immerses. A lesser level of impurity exists in a zav and a nidda, for in them too the impurity comes out from something that could have produced life and died, and they are considered "avot ha-tum'a." The zav, the zava and the nidda become pure by counting seven days and immersing, without sprinkling of the water of the ashes of the red heifer.

A person or vessel that touched an av ha-tum'a, that is, a zav or nidda or a person who became impure from a corpse, becomes impure, and after immersing and when the day ends, becomes pure. A neveila (animal carcass) or a dead sheretz (creeping creature) is also impure at the level of av ha-tum'a, and a person or vessel touching them becomes impure, and in order to become pure must immerse, and when the day ends becomes pure. Vessels made of stone or earth do not contract impurity.

The teruma produce must also be protected from becoming impure. If, after being picked, it became wet with one of the seven liquids (water, wine, honey, olive oil, milk, dew, blood), it is rendered susceptible to impurity, and if an impure person touches it, even after it has dried, it becomes impure. But if it did not become wet, it is not rendered susceptible to impurity, and even if an impure person or an impure vessel touches it, it does not become impure.

Although the terumot are meant to be eaten by kohanim in purity, even when the produce has become impure one is obligated to separate terumot from it, as it is stated (Bamidbar 18:8): "And I, behold, I have given you the charge of My terumot" – "both pure teruma and impure teruma." When the teruma is pure it is meant for eating, and when it is impure it must be burned, and it is preferable that the kohen benefit from it while burning it: if it is produce, he should heat the oven with it, and if it is oil, he should light lamps with it (Shabbat 25a; Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 2:14-15).

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: The Difference between the Kohanim and the Levites
sections.html:
For most of the year, the kohanim and Levites lived in their own cities throughout the land, and when their family's turn came to serve in the Temple, they would go up to Jerusalem. The main burden of the Temple service and the sacrifices was placed on the kohanim, while the Levites assisted them in two roles: 1) guarding the gates of the Temple; 2) accompanying the offering of the communal sacrifices with song and music. For this purpose the Levites established choirs and orchestras. When the kohanim and Levites were in the Temple, the kohanim were sustained by the portions of the sacrificial meat designated for them, and by the menaḥot (meal-offerings) and the bikkurim (first fruits). The Levites, on the other hand, were sustained by the fruit of ma'aser sheni that the Israelites brought up to Jerusalem, as it is stated (Devarim 14:26-27): "And you shall eat there before the Lord your God, and you shall rejoice, you and your household. And the Levite who is within your gates, you shall not forsake him, for he has no portion or inheritance with you." And also from the meat of the shelamim (peace-offerings) and of ma'aser behema (the animal tithe) that the Israelites offered, as it is stated (ibid. 12:18-19): "But you shall eat them before the Lord your God in the place which the Lord your God shall choose, you and your son and your daughter, and your manservant and your maidservant, and the Levite who is within your gates; and you shall rejoice before the Lord your God in all that you put your hand to. Take heed to yourself that you do not forsake the Levite as long as you live upon your land."

For most of the year, while they lived in their homes, the kohanim were sustained by the terumot and the Levites by ma'aser rishon. And the Torah commanded that the Levites separate terumat ma'aser from their tithes for the kohen, and thereby the bond between the Levites and the kohanim was strengthened.

There is a significant difference between the kohanim and the Levites, for the terumot are holy and it is forbidden to eat them in impurity, whereas the tithe for the Levite is ḥullin (non-sacred) and may be eaten in impurity. It follows that their way of life was different: the kohanim and their families had to be careful at all times not to become impure, whereas the Levites, like the rest of Israel, were careful to purify themselves only before going up to the Temple, but the rest of the time they did not need to guard against impurity. Thus the kohanim needed to conduct themselves with extra separateness, and their role was to extend the holiness of the Temple throughout the land, and from within such an atmosphere to teach Torah to Israel. The Levites, on the other hand, came into closer contact with the Israelites, and presumably were more engaged in teaching and educating children. Since the Levites did not need to guard against impurity, they could, when necessary, work at additional occupations. By contrast, the kohanim received many gifts, some of them while they served in the Temple, and thereby they could extend their stay in Jerusalem. They also received throughout the land important gifts that had no sanctity, such as the foreleg, the cheeks and the maw of every animal slaughtered, so that they could sustain themselves even when they were impure. For there were times when the kohanim too became impure, for example when relatives of theirs died, and also women in their days of impurity and men in their days of zav discharge; and even one who had marital relations or had a seminal emission was not permitted to eat teruma before immersing and the day ending. In any case, relative to their number at the beginning of the nation's history, the kohanim received many more gifts than the Levites. Apparently this led to the kohanim increasing in number relatively more than the Levites. And it is possible that this was the Torah's intention: to strengthen the priesthood, which tended towards piety and purity, relative to the Levites. At the beginning of the Second Temple period, a situation had already arisen in which the number of kohanim who came up to the Land was ten times that of the Levites.4

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Ma'aser Rishon
sections.html:
The Torah commands that ma'aser rishon be given to the Levite and not to the kohen. Although the kohanim are also members of the tribe of Levi, and when kohanim have tevel produce, after separating ma'aser rishon they keep it themselves and separate terumat ma'aser from it for themselves, nonetheless, when an Israelite has produce, he must give the ma'aser rishon specifically to a Levite (following Rabbi Akiva in Yevamot 86a-b; Yerushalmi Ma'aser Sheni 5:3; Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 1:1).

At the beginning of the Second Temple period, Ezra asked the Levites to come up to the Land, but only a few of them came up, fewer than a tenth of the number of kohanim and less than one percent of all those who came up. Ezra penalized the Levites, so that one would not be obligated to give them all of the ma'aser rishon, which is about nine percent of all the produce. For the tithe is given to them in return for their service, as it is stated (Bamidbar 18:21): "And to the children of Levi, behold, I have given all the tithe in Israel for an inheritance, in return for their service which they serve," and not in order to make them wealthy. Therefore it was established that the tithe could also be given to the kohanim, as well as to other needs that the beit din would determine. The beit din was able to impose this penalty because ma'aser rishon is property that has no sanctity, and it is within the authority of the beit din to expropriate it from the Levites and give it to whomever it determines. In the Jerusalem Talmud (Ma'aser Sheni 5:5) it is explained that at first they enacted that the tithe be brought to the Temple treasury: a third of it was given to the kohanim and Levites who were in Jerusalem, a third was left in the treasury for public needs in Jerusalem, and a third was distributed to the poor and Torah scholars in Jerusalem. It seems that when the Jewish settlement expanded, they went back to distributing ma'aser rishon throughout the land, except that as a result of the penalty, instead of giving it only to the Levites, they gave it to the kohanim as well (Yevamot 86b, according to Tosafot, Rosh and others).

Some say that the penalty was annulled after the destruction of the Second Temple, and since then ma'aser rishon must be given specifically to Levites, and this is the proper practice (Beit Yosef and SA YD 331:19, based on Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 1:4).5

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Ma'aser Sheni
sections.html:
After separating ma'aser rishon for the Levite, it is a mitzva to separate another tithe from the remaining produce, which is about 9% of all the produce that there was at first. In years 1, 2, 4 and 5 of the Shemita cycle one separates ma'aser sheni, and in years 3 and 6 one separates ma'aser ani. What is special about ma'aser sheni is that even though it has sanctity and is called "mamon gavo'ah" (property of the Most High), it remains in the possession of the owner of the produce, and he is commanded to eat it with his family within the walls of Jerusalem in purity. As it is stated (Devarim 14:22-23): "You shall surely tithe all the produce of your seed that the field brings forth year by year. And you shall eat before the Lord your God, in the place which He shall choose to cause His name to dwell there, the tithe of your grain, your wine and your oil… so that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always."

Those who find it difficult to bring the fruit of ma'aser sheni up to Jerusalem because of the distance and the large quantity of produce may redeem it with money, so that the produce becomes ḥullin and the sanctity passes to the money, which they take up to Jerusalem and with which they buy food and eat it in purity according to the law of eating ma'aser sheni. As it is stated (ibid. 24-26): "And if the way is too long for you, so that you are not able to carry it, because the place which the Lord your God shall choose to set His name there is too far from you, when the Lord your God blesses you; then you shall turn it into money, and bind up the money in your hand, and go to the place which the Lord your God shall choose. And you shall spend the money on whatever your soul desires, on cattle, or on sheep, or on wine, or on strong drink, or on whatever your soul asks of you; and you shall eat there before the Lord your God, and you shall rejoice, you and your household."

At the time of redemption, one must add a fifth to the value of the produce, as it is stated (Vayikra 27:30-31): "And all the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the tree, is the Lord's; it is holy to the Lord. And if a man wishes to redeem any of his tithe, he shall add to it a fifth of it." This fifth is calculated on the total, that is, one must add a quarter to the price of the produce, so that in the total calculation the addition will be a fifth. For example: if the price of the produce is 100, with the addition of the fifth it will be 125.

The fruit of ma'aser sheni is holy, and it is forbidden to treat it as ḥullin, for example by selling it or exchanging it.6

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: The Meaning of Ma'aser Sheni
sections.html:
Through the fruit of ma'aser sheni all Israel was strengthened in the mitzva of aliya la-regel (pilgrimage) – on the festival of Matzot, the festival of Shavuot and the festival of Sukkot. For the mitzva required eating in Jerusalem about six percent of the entire yield of the fields during the six working years of the Shemita cycle, and the suitable time for this was at the festival meals. And the mitzva was to include Levites and poor people in the meals as well, and the more blessing a person merited, the more he merited to lengthen his family's stay in the shadow of the Shekhina in Jerusalem, and to host more Levites and poor people at his meal. And if he had children who could engage in Torah study, he would encourage them to remain in Jerusalem to study Torah there and to eat from the money of ma'aser sheni, as it is stated (Devarim 14:23): "So that you may learn to fear the Lord your God" – "this tells us that the tithe brings a person to Torah study" (Sifrei Re'eh 106; Tosafot Bava Batra 21a, s.v. "Ki").

On the one hand, one who had difficulty going up for the nearby festivals could keep the money of the ma'aser sheni produce with him until the festival at which he would merit to go up. But on the other hand, it is impossible to postpone eating it without limit, for the Torah set a time by which one is obligated to finish the ma'aser sheni, and that is the time of "bi'ur ma'asrot" (the removal of tithes) (as explained in halakha 12).7

The mitzva of ma'aser behema was also intended to connect Israel to the Temple (below 19:9). Thus, at the time of aliya la-regel, Israel was sustained by the fruit of ma'aser sheni and the food they bought with its redemption money, and by the meat of the ma'aser behema sacrifice. And the more blessing they merited, the more people they included in their meal. Thus ma'aser sheni and ma'aser behema were a kind of spiritual "study fund," intended for aliya la-regel and staying in Jerusalem.

From the fact that the same tithe served for four years as ma'aser sheni and for two years as ma'aser ani, one can learn that holiness and giving to the poor are one matter. Indeed, it is a special mitzva for those who have ma'aser sheni and ma'aser behema to include the poor in the joy of their meal (see Peninei Halakha: Mo'adim 1:11, n. 6).

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Ma'aser Ani
sections.html:
In the third and sixth years of the Shemita cycle, it is a mitzva to give a tithe to the poor instead of ma'aser sheni, as it is stated (Devarim 14:28-29): "At the end of every three years you shall bring forth all the tithe of your produce in that year, and lay it up within your gates. And the Levite (this refers to a poor Levite), because he has no portion or inheritance with you, and the stranger, and the orphan, and the widow who are within your gates, shall come and eat and be satisfied, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all the work of your hand which you do" (and likewise in Devarim 26:12). Thus the cycle of the second tithe consists of three years: in the first two years, ma'aser sheni, and in the third year, ma'aser ani. Ma'aser ani has no sanctity, and the poor person may eat it wherever he wishes, and may also sell it.

The place for distributing the tithes is in the field after the gathering of the produce has been completed (above halakha 5). It is a mitzva to give each of the poor enough to satisfy him, that is, the value of the food for two meals that people were accustomed to eat each day, as it is stated: "That they may eat within your gates and be satisfied." To a married man one also gives enough to satisfy his wife and young children. When the tithe does not contain a satisfying amount for each of the poor, one places the tithe before the poor and they divide it among themselves. If he gave each of the poor who came to his field enough to satisfy him and he still had tithe produce left over, he may give them more than enough to satisfy them until he finishes the whole tithe, or he may keep the remainder for his poor relatives, on condition that he does not keep for them more than half of the tithe (Mishna Pe'a 8:5, and Yerushalmi there). If the poor did not come to the field, and the owner of the produce needed to bring it to the poor, he has tovat hana'a in it, meaning that he may distribute it to the poor person of his choice. And if he has poor relatives, he may give them the entire tithe (Nedarim 84b; Rambam, Hilkhot Matanot Aniyim 6:7-13).

Seemingly it is difficult: why did the Torah establish that ma'aser sheni be separated in years 1, 2, 4 and 5 and ma'aser ani in years 3 and 6? If it wished to encourage pilgrimage and also to help the poor, why did it not command that every single year two-thirds be dedicated to pilgrimage and one-third to the poor? If the poor need additional help, why give it to them only for two years out of a cycle of seven years? Apparently, the Torah's intention is that the poor should receive help for their basic subsistence through leket, shikheḥa and pe'a, and additional tzedaka as needed. Ma'aser ani, by contrast, is intended to grant them good years in which they can enjoy prosperity. In addition, it can be hoped that, insofar as it is within their power, the prosperity of these years will motivate the poor or their children to be more diligent and efficient in their work in the other years, so that they will break out of the cycle of poverty and merit prosperity and independence. But if they received a moderate allowance every year, they would become accustomed to making do with it, without its giving them any special joy, and without a desire to change their situation growing in their souls during the years of want.

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: The Mitzva of Bi'ur Ma'asrot
sections.html:
The tithe cycle consists of two series of three years. In all the years one separates terumot and ma'aser rishon, but ma'aser sheni and ma'aser ani alternate. In the first and second years one separates ma'aser sheni, and in the third, ma'aser ani. Likewise in the second series: in the fourth and fifth years ma'aser sheni, and in the sixth ma'aser ani. In the seventh year the produce is ownerless, and consequently terumot u-ma'asrot are not separated from it.

After each cycle of three years, it is a mitzva to complete the separation of the terumot u-ma'asrot and to distribute them, and this is the mitzva of "bi'ur ma'asrot," as it is stated (Devarim 14:28): "At the end of every three years you shall bring forth all the tithe of your produce in that year, and lay it up within your gates." That is, by the time of bi'ur one is obligated to complete the separation of the terumot u-ma'asrot from the produce of the three past years, and to give the terumot and ḥalla to the kohen, the ma'aser rishon to the Levite, and the ma'aser ani to the poor person, and to bring the fruit of ma'aser sheni and neta reva'i (fourth-year fruit) up to Jerusalem and eat them in purity. One who did not manage to bring them up to Jerusalem and the time of bi'ur arrived must remove them from his possession by burning or by another method that destroys them from the world. The kohen, the Levite and the poor person are not obligated to finish eating the gifts in their possession by the end of the time of bi'ur, for by the fact that they came into their possession before the time of bi'ur the mitzva was fulfilled with them (Yerushalmi Bikkurim 2:2, Rash Sirilio; Sha'arei Tzedek 11:22).

The time of bi'ur is at the end of the festival of Pesaḥ following the completion of the three years, that is, on Pesaḥ of the fourth year and on Pesaḥ of the seventh year. This is because the fruit of trees that grows by virtue of the rains of the third year reaches ḥanata (the initial fruit-formation stage) by Tu Bi-Shvat of the fourth year, and its picking is completed towards the festival of Pesaḥ of the fourth year; it follows that only on Pesaḥ of the fourth year is it possible to finish all the tithes of the third year. However, grain, legumes and vegetables that became obligated in tithes in the fourth year before Pesaḥ belong to the fourth year, and consequently the bi'ur of their tithes is on Pesaḥ of the seventh year (Yerushalmi Ma'aser Sheni 5:3; 5:5; Rambam 11:7).8

The mitzva of bi'ur was especially beneficial for ma'aser sheni and neta reva'i, which had to be brought up to Jerusalem; since pilgrimage involved difficulties, and many people had reasons to be exempt from it, they could have kept the redemption money and postponed without limit the time of pilgrimage and of eating the food that must be bought with its money. Therefore the Torah set a time by which one must remove the redemption money of the ma'aser sheni and neta reva'i. If he manages to go up to Jerusalem and eat food bought with their money by the time of bi'ur – very good; if not, he can give them to his relatives or friends so that they may enjoy them in Jerusalem; and if not, he is obligated to destroy them by the time of bi'ur. With regard to the terumot and the tithes for the Levite and the poor, there are additional mitzvot that set earlier times for giving them (below halakha 14).

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: The Mitzva of Viduy Ma'asrot
sections.html:
It is a mitzva for one who has removed his tithes from his house according to halakha to make a declaration about this before God at Minḥa of the last Yom Tov of Pesaḥ in the fourth and seventh years of the Shemita cycle (Mishna Ma'aser Sheni 5:10). As it is stated (Devarim 26:12-15): "When you have finished tithing all the tithe of your produce in the third year, the year of tithing… then you shall say before the Lord your God (this formula): I have removed the holy things from the house, and I have also given them to the Levite, and to the stranger, to the orphan and to the widow, according to all Your commandment which You have commanded me; I have not transgressed any of Your commandments, nor have I forgotten them. I have not eaten of it in my mourning, nor have I removed any of it while impure, nor given any of it for the dead; I have listened to the voice of the Lord my God, I have done according to all that You have commanded me. Look down from Your holy habitation, from heaven, and bless Your people Israel, and the land which You have given us, as You swore to our fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey." From the fact that the Sages called this mitzva "viduy ma'asrot" (the confession of tithes), we learn that there is also a positive viduy about mitzvot, for the viduy is a summing up of matters before God. It is a mitzva to say the viduy in the Temple, as it is stated (ibid. 13): "Then you shall say before the Lord your God." However, one who did not merit to make the pilgrimage at the time of bi'ur had to say the viduy where he was. One who does not understand Hebrew may say it in translation (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser Sheni 11:5-6).

Only one who did not transgress any of the laws of terumot u-ma'asrot during the three years is entitled to say the viduy, as it is stated: "I have removed the holy things from the house, and I have also given them to the Levite, and to the stranger, to the orphan and to the widow, according to all Your commandment which You have commanded me" – that he gave all the gifts and did not change the order of their separation. "I have not transgressed any of Your commandments" – that he did not separate from one species on behalf of another species, nor from detached produce on behalf of attached produce, nor from attached on behalf of detached, nor from new on behalf of old, nor from old on behalf of new. "Nor have I forgotten them" – that he did not forget to recite the blessing before fulfilling the mitzva. "I have not eaten of it in my mourning" – that he did not eat ma'aser sheni while he was an onen (a mourner before the burial). "Nor have I removed any of it while impure" – that he did not make it impure. "Nor given any of it for the dead" – that he did not use the redemption money of ma'aser sheni for other mitzvot, even for the burial of the dead. "I have listened to the voice of the Lord my God" – that he brought the ma'aser sheni up to the Chosen House. "I have done according to all that You have commanded me" – that he rejoiced and made others rejoice with it, as it is stated (Devarim 26:11): "And you shall rejoice in all the good which the Lord your God has given you and your household, you, and the Levite, and the stranger who is in your midst" (Mishna Ma'aser Sheni 5:11-12; Rambam 11:15).

After a person has merited to fulfill the mitzva of terumot u-ma'asrot in all its details and fine points, the people of Israel can be blessed in his merit, except that without prayer the blessing will not come; therefore he is commanded to pray and request: "Look down from Your holy habitation, from heaven, and bless Your people Israel, and the land which You have given us, as You swore to our fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey."

Nowadays, viduy ma'asrot is not said, because the Temple has been destroyed and we cannot eat ma'aser sheni produce in purity in Jerusalem as the Torah commands. Some have the custom to make a remembrance of the mitzva, and they read from the Torah the entire passage in which the verses of the viduy appear.9

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: The Time of the Obligation to Separate and Distribute Terumot u-Ma'asrot
sections.html:
The owner of the produce is commanded not to wait until the time of bi'ur, but immediately after he finishes gathering his produce from the field, he should separate terumot u-ma'asrot and distribute them as the Torah commands, for when a mitzva comes your way, do not let it become stale (Mekhilta de-Rabbi Yishmael, Parashat Bo 9).

Admittedly, as long as one of the three pilgrimage festivals has not passed, he has not yet neglected a positive commandment; but if one of the three pilgrimage festivals has passed and he has not given his gifts, he has neglected a positive commandment. For it is stated regarding one who pledged to offer a sacrifice, or one who had ma'aser sheni or ma'aser behema, that together with the mitzva of pilgrimage he is commanded to bring his sacrifices and his tithes, as it is stated (Devarim 12:5-6): "And there you shall come, and there you shall bring your burnt-offerings and your sacrifices, and your tithes, and the teruma of your hand." However, one who was exempt from pilgrimage, for example because he was ill, did not neglect a mitzva by not bringing up the sacrifices he had pledged and the ma'aser behema at the first festival.

And if three pilgrimage festivals have passed and he has not brought them, he has transgressed a negative prohibition, as it is stated (ibid. 23:22-24): "When you make a vow to the Lord your God, you shall not delay to pay it, for the Lord your God will surely require it of you, and it would be sin in you… That which has gone out of your lips you shall keep…" The Sages explained that after three festivals he is considered one who has delayed paying it, and this is the law regarding terumot for the kohen and tithes for the Levite and the poor (Rosh Ha-shana 4a; Tosafot s.v. "Tzedakot," "U-ma'asrot"; Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aseh Ha-korbanot 14:13).

In addition, as we learned (in halakha 12), with regard to terumot u-ma'asrot there is a special mitzva – bi'ur ma'asrot – whose purpose is to complete the fulfillment of the mitzva of separating terumot u-ma'asrot from all the produce of the first three years of the Shemita cycle by Pesaḥ of the fourth year, and of years 4, 5 and 6 of the Shemita cycle by Pesaḥ of the seventh year.10

[Video in the original Hebrew page]

sections.title: Bikkurim
sections.html:
There was another mitzva when the Temple stood: to bring the bikkurim (first fruits) to the kohanim in the Temple. This is the order of fulfilling the mitzva of bringing the bikkurim: every Jew who has a field in the Land of Israel and grows in it fruit of the seven species, when he sees the first fruits at the beginning of their growth, should mark them with a thread and say: "These are bikkurim," and when they ripen he should pick them, place them in a beautiful vessel and bring them up to Jerusalem. As it is stated (Devarim 26:1-11): "And it shall be, when you come into the land which the Lord your God gives you for an inheritance, and you possess it and dwell in it, that you shall take of the first of all the fruit of the ground which you bring in from your land that the Lord your God gives you, and you shall put it in a basket, and go to the place which the Lord your God shall choose to cause His name to dwell there. And you shall come to the kohen who shall be in those days and say to him: I declare this day to the Lord your God that I have come to the land which the Lord swore to our fathers to give us." Then the kohen, together with the owner of the bikkurim, would wave the bikkurim fruit, as it is stated: "And the kohen shall take the basket from your hand and set it down before the altar of the Lord your God." And the owner of the bikkurim would recite the text of "Mikra Bikkurim" (the declaration of the first fruits), which contains the story of the people of Israel: "And you shall respond and say before the Lord your God: An Aramean sought to destroy my father, and he went down to Egypt and sojourned there, few in number, and there he became a nation, great, mighty and numerous. And the Egyptians dealt ill with us and afflicted us and laid upon us hard labor. And we cried to the Lord, the God of our fathers, and the Lord heard our voice and saw our affliction, our toil and our oppression. And the Lord brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, with great awe, with signs and with wonders. And He brought us to this place and gave us this land, a land flowing with milk and honey. And now, behold, I have brought the first of the fruit of the ground which You, O Lord, have given me." Afterwards the owner of the bikkurim would place the fruit beside the altar, and the kohen would take it and eat it in holiness. Together with fulfilling the mitzva of bringing the bikkurim, there was a mitzva to bow down before God and to rejoice by offering shelamim. As it is stated: "And you shall set it down before the Lord your God and bow down before the Lord your God. And you shall rejoice in all the good which the Lord your God has given you and your household, you, and the Levite, and the stranger who is in your midst." It was a mitzva to stay at least one more night in Jerusalem, and only the next day was the Israelite permitted to return home (Rambam, Hilkhot Bikkurim 3:10-14).

The mitzva of bringing up the bikkurim was performed with great splendor and joy. The pilgrims would gather in caravans, and when they approached Jerusalem, people from Jerusalem would go out to meet them and enter the city with them in song, accompanied by musical instruments. From the time they reached the Temple Mount, the owner of the bikkurim had to carry the fruit on his shoulder, and when they entered the Temple courtyard, the Levites would begin to sing and play, until they handed the bikkurim to the kohanim (Mishna Bikkurim 3:1-6; Rambam 3:10-14).

By Torah law, bikkurim are brought only from the western side of the Jordan, which is "a land flowing with milk and honey," and by rabbinic law they are brought also from the eastern side of the Jordan and from Syria (Rambam, Hilkhot Bikkurim 1:1). By Torah law, bikkurim have no fixed amount, and the Sages enacted that one should separate one-sixtieth for bikkurim, and one who wishes to add may add without limit (Rambam 2:17). The law of bikkurim is like that of teruma, in that only the families of kohanim were permitted to eat them, in purity; however, unlike terumot, which are eaten throughout the land, the place for eating bikkurim is only within the walls of the city of Jerusalem (ibid. 3:3-5). The time for bringing bikkurim ab initio is from the festival of Shavuot until Sukkot, for that is the time when the fruit of the seven species ripens and people rejoice in its growth. One who did not bring them by Sukkot may, after the fact, bring them until Ḥanuka, but he does not recite Mikra Bikkurim (ibid. 1:6; 4:13).

The idea in the mitzva of bikkurim is that in everything one must first give expression to the sacred ideal. Therefore the first fruits of the choicest species must be brought up to Jerusalem to the kohanim. And through this, the indwelling of the Shekhina can be drawn into all the works of Israel's hands throughout the land and in all areas of life, so that they will be full of values and meaning, blessing and joy. (This idea finds expression in various ways also in the mitzva of firstborns, as explained below 19:4; ḥadash, as explained above 1:1-2; and neta reva'i, as explained above 2:2.)
